newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says needle reuse led to hepatitis outbreaks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says needle reuse led to hepatitis outbreaks.

text.p: Two outbreaks of hepatitis B virus infection in a nursing home and hospital occurred because a fingerstick device for obtaining blood samples was used for more than one patient, federal health officials said Thursday.
The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said the outbreaks last year involved 11 residents of an Ohio nursing home and 14 patients at a New York City hospital.
The fingerstick devices were used to draw blood to measure glucose in patients with diabetes. The nursing home and the hospital stopped using the devices after the outbreaks.
After a similar outbreak in 1990, the CDC and the Food and Drug Administration recommended that the devices only be used for a single patient.

Hepatitis B is a serious disease caused by a virus that attacks the liver. The virus can be transmitted through cuts and needle pricks. The CDC said it can survive in a dried state on medical devices for at least a week.
More than 200,000 people of all ages get hepatitis B every year and almost 5,000 die of illnesses related to the virus, health officials said.
